a.title: What Is Physical Commodity Trading?
a.desc: The difference between physical and paper markets — why a cargo is not a futures contract.
a.hook: Most people think commodity trading is about predicting where prices go. The traders who actually make money know it's about something else entirely.
paragraphs: When a commodity trader executes a deal, they are not placing a bet on a price chart. They are arranging the physical movement of a real substance — a cargo of LNG on a vessel 400 nautical miles off Singapore, a parcel of crude already loaded at Ras Tanura, a batch of gasoil sitting in a tank farm in Rotterdam — from where it is to where it needs to be, at a price that makes the journey worthwhile.

This is **physical trading**. It involves a vessel, a loading port, a delivery window, a cargo specification, a counterparty who actually needs the molecules, and an operations team making sure the whole chain executes on time. The **paper market** — futures on ICE or NYMEX, swaps, options — exists alongside the physical market but is not the same thing. A paper position can be opened and closed in seconds. A physical cargo cannot.

The two markets are deeply connected — physical traders use paper instruments to hedge price exposure, and paper markets are anchored to physical price assessments — but the disciplines are different. A physical trader needs to understand freight, cargo specs, laytime, demurrage, and credit. Most major commodity firms do both, but the commercial logic of the desk starts with the physical.

Physical trading is logistics with a P&L attached. Every barrel has to be somewhere, on something, going somewhere else — and the gap between what it costs to move it and what someone will pay for it when it arrives is where the money is made.

Whether you are entering a trading role, an analytics function, or a scheduling position, understanding the physical market is the baseline. The desk measures everything against physical reality — cargo availability, vessel positions, terminal throughput. Speak that language and you can follow the commercial logic behind every desk decision.
a.pullQuote: Physical trading is logistics with a P&L attached. Every barrel has to be somewhere, on something, going somewhere else — and the gap between what it costs to move it and what someone will pay for it when it arrives is where the money is made.

a.title: The Energy Markets Landscape
a.desc: Oil, LNG, natural gas, and power — how each market is structured and how they connect.
a.hook: Commodity trading is not one industry. It is four overlapping industries that share infrastructure, pricing signals, and often the same desk.
paragraphs: The energy commodity market is commonly discussed as if it were a single entity — but in practice it is four distinct markets, each with its own pricing structure, physical infrastructure, and commercial logic. **Crude oil and refined products** form the largest and most liquid market. Crude is extracted, shipped to refineries, and converted into gasoline, gasoil, jet fuel, fuel oil, and naphtha. Each product has its own market, benchmark, and demand drivers.

**LNG** — liquefied natural gas — is the fastest-growing segment. Natural gas is supercooled to liquid at -162°C, loaded onto specialised carriers, and shipped globally. Key benchmarks are JKM (Japan Korea Marker) for Asian spot prices and TTF for European gas. The JKM/TTF spread determines whether Atlantic Basin cargoes flow east or stay in Europe — one of the most important arbitrage signals in commodity markets today.

**Pipeline gas** is geographically constrained — it cannot be rerouted the way a ship can. **Power markets** sit at the end of the chain, converting primary energy into electricity. Each commodity feeds into the next: an Australian LNG export drop affects European TTF, which affects coal-to-gas switching, which affects CO2 prices. Learning to trace these connections is the commercial analyst's core skill.

Energy markets are not separate silos. When Australian LNG exports drop, it affects European TTF prices, which affects coal-to-gas switching in power, which affects carbon prices. Tracing these connections is what separates a market reader from a news reader.

When you read about a refinery outage, trace it to product supply, then crude demand, then freight for vessels heading there. When you read about a cold snap in Northeast Asia, trace it to LNG demand, JKM prices, then Atlantic cargo flows. The market is always a chain of connected reactions.
a.pullQuote: Energy markets are not separate silos. When Australian LNG exports drop, it affects European TTF prices, which affects coal-to-gas switching in power, which affects carbon prices. Tracing these connections is what separates a market reader from a news reader.
a.handoff: Now that you can see the markets — how does a trading desk actually make money across all of them?

a.title: How a Trade Makes Money
a.desc: The six revenue levers a commodity trader pulls — flat price, time spread, location, quality, freight, optionality.
a.hook: Most people assume commodity trading profit comes from buying low and selling high on flat price. Most commodity trading profit does not come from that at all.
paragraphs: Flat price — the outright price of crude or a product — is one source of revenue. But for most physical commodity desks, it is not the primary one. The reason is simple: flat price is the most competed, most watched signal in the market. Everyone has a view on where Brent is going. The real commercial edge comes from signals that are harder to read, faster to act on, and less efficiently priced.

There are six distinct levers a physical desk pulls. **Flat price**: buying low, selling high — the simplest but most competed. **Time spread**: exploiting price differences between delivery dates. A contango market rewards storage; backwardation rewards selling promptly. **Location differential**: the price gap between two regions. Moving a cargo from where it is cheap to where it is expensive, if freight allows.

**Quality differential**: different crude grades and product specs trade at different prices. Sourcing the right grade at the right differential for a specific refinery is a skill in itself. **Freight**: locking in cheap shipping before the market tightens generates P&L from the differential between what you pay and what the market moves to. **Optionality**: a cargo with flexible loading window or destination flexibility is worth more. Desks that structure optionality into positions earn when conditions change.

The best trades are the ones where you are right on three levers at once — the location arb is open, the time spread is working in your favour, and you have the freight locked before anyone else. That is when you make real money.

When you review a commodity trade or a market scenario, identify which of the six levers it is using — and which it is not. Most trades combine two or three levers simultaneously. Understanding which levers a desk is long or short on any given day is the foundation of commercial awareness that hiring managers test for.
a.pullQuote: The best trades are the ones where you are right on three levers at once — the location arb is open, the time spread is working in your favour, and you have the freight locked before anyone else. That is when you make real money.

a.title: Refinery Economics & Crack Spreads
a.desc: Crude slate, product yields, and what the crack spread signals to the desk.
a.hook: A refinery does not just convert crude oil into products. It converts the price difference between crude and products into margin — and that margin tells the market something important every single day.
paragraphs: The refinery sits at the centre of the oil value chain. It buys crude at one price, processes it through distillation, cracking, and treating units, and sells the resulting products — gasoline, gasoil, jet fuel, fuel oil, naphtha — at a higher price. The difference between the revenue from products and the cost of crude input is the **crack spread** — the refinery's gross margin.

The standard benchmark is the **3-2-1 crack spread**: three barrels of crude yield two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillate. The formula is (2 × gasoline price + 1 × distillate price − 3 × crude price) ÷ 3. At $95/bbl gasoline, $90/bbl distillate, and $75/bbl crude, the 3-2-1 crack is $18.33/bbl. After operating costs of roughly $5–8/bbl, the net refinery margin is around $10–13/bbl.

What makes crack spreads commercially important is what they signal. A **widening crack** signals strong product demand or tight crude supply — refiners are earning well and running hard. A **compressing crack** signals oversupply in products or a crude price spike that hasn't passed through to consumers yet. Refiners respond by adjusting run rates — which directly affects how much crude they buy and how much product hits the market.

The crack spread doesn't just tell you if refining is profitable — it tells you which direction the physical market is about to move. A refiner cutting runs today is tightening product supply in three weeks.

Check crack spreads before reading headline crude prices. If cracks are compressing while crude rallies, the rally may not hold — refiners will pull back demand. If cracks are widening while crude is flat, watch for product-led price action. The crack is the leading indicator; flat price often follows.
a.pullQuote: The crack spread doesn't just tell you if refining is profitable — it tells you which direction the physical market is about to move. A refiner cutting runs today is tightening product supply in three weeks.

a.title: Shipping, Freight & Cargo Economics
a.desc: Vessel classes, freight rate mechanics, laytime, and how freight changes the arbitrage calculus.
a.hook: Freight is not just a cost in commodity trading. It is a variable that can open or close an arbitrage window overnight — and a source of P&L in its own right.
paragraphs: Every physical commodity trade involves transportation. The economics of that transportation — vessel class, freight rate, route, speed, port costs — directly determine whether a trade is viable. A **VLCC** (Very Large Crude Carrier) carries 2 million barrels of crude and is used on long-haul routes like Middle East Gulf to Asia or the Americas. A **Suezmax** carries around 1 million barrels and is sized to transit the Suez Canal. An **Aframax** carries 500,000–750,000 barrels on shorter regional routes. LNG carriers are entirely different — purpose-built, insulated, and carrying between 125,000 and 210,000 cubic metres of liquefied gas.

Freight rates are quoted in **Worldscale** points for tankers — a percentage of a standard rate that accounts for vessel size and route — or in $/day for time charters. The Baltic Exchange publishes the key indices: the BDTI (Baltic Dirty Tanker Index) for crude tankers, the BCTI (Baltic Clean Tanker Index) for product tankers, and the BLNG for LNG carriers. When freight rates rise, the cost of moving a cargo increases — which narrows any arbitrage spread and may make a previously viable trade uneconomic.

**Laytime** is the time allowed for loading or discharging a cargo under the charter party. If the vessel exceeds this time, the charterer pays **demurrage** — typically $20,000–$60,000 per day for a VLCC. If loading completes early, the owner may pay **dispatch**. Laytime calculations depend on NOR (Notice of Readiness) tendering, port congestion, weather exceptions, and the specific charter party terms — and disputes over demurrage are extremely common.

The arbitrage calc is the easy part. The hard part is knowing whether the freight you need is actually available at the rate you assumed — and whether it will still be open by the time your cargo arrives.

Always run your freight assumption before committing to a physical trade. A 10% freight rate move on a VLCC changes the economics of a long-haul crude arbitrage by $0.30–$0.50/bbl. On a 2 million barrel cargo, that is $600,000–$1 million of P&L difference. Freight is never just a cost line.
a.pullQuote: The arbitrage calc is the easy part. The hard part is knowing whether the freight you need is actually available at the rate you assumed — and whether it will still be open by the time your cargo arrives.

a.title: Storage, Terminals & the Inventory Signal
a.desc: What tank levels and floating storage tell a trader about supply balance.
a.hook: The EIA inventory report comes out every Wednesday at 10:30am New York time. What the desk looks for in those 90 seconds tells you everything about how physical traders actually read the market.
paragraphs: Physical commodity storage is the buffer between supply and demand. When supply exceeds demand, inventory builds — in tank farms, pipelines, and increasingly in vessels used as floating storage. When demand exceeds supply, inventories draw. The level and direction of inventory change is one of the most reliable signals of physical market balance available to a trader.

The **EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report** is released every Wednesday and covers US crude and product inventories — crude stocks, gasoline, distillates, and refinery inputs. The market watches the crude draw or build against analyst consensus. A draw that beats expectations — say, a 4.2 million barrel draw against a consensus estimate of 1.8 million barrels — is a bullish signal. But the desk also watches **days of forward cover** (how many days of consumption current stocks represent), refinery utilisation rates, and the split between commercial stocks and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

**Floating storage** — vessels anchored and used as storage rather than in transit — appears when the contango in the forward curve is large enough to cover vessel hire costs plus insurance and financing. During COVID in 2020, floating storage reached record levels as onshore tanks filled and the curve went into extreme contango. Tracking floating storage via AIS data gives traders a real-time read on supply balance that is not captured in any official inventory report.

The inventory signal is not the number — it is the number relative to the expectation, relative to the seasonal norm, and relative to what the price already moved in anticipation. All three together tell you whether the signal is real.

When reading an EIA report, never focus only on the headline crude number. Check the product split, the refinery utilisation rate, and the import/export flows. And always compare to the 5-year seasonal average — a 3 million barrel build in March is very different from the same build in August when seasonal patterns diverge sharply.
a.pullQuote: The inventory signal is not the number — it is the number relative to the expectation, relative to the seasonal norm, and relative to what the price already moved in anticipation. All three together tell you whether the signal is real.

a.title: The Role of Price Reporting Agencies
a.desc: How Platts and Argus assess prices — and why the last 30 minutes of the window moves markets.
a.hook: Every day at a specific time, a small team of price reporters at Platts and Argus publish benchmark prices that govern trillions of dollars of commodity contracts globally. Understanding how they do it explains something important about how physical commodity markets actually work.
paragraphs: Physical commodity prices are not set by an exchange. Unlike crude futures on ICE or NYMEX, which are traded continuously in an open market, physical prices for crude grades, refined products, and LNG are assessed by **Price Reporting Agencies** (PRAs) — primarily Platts (now S&P Global Commodity Insights), Argus Media, and ICIS. These assessments are then used as reference prices in billions of dollars of physical supply contracts and financial derivatives.

The dominant methodology is the **Market on Close (MOC)** process, used by Platts for crude and products. During a defined assessment window — typically the last 30 minutes of the trading day — reporters gather bids, offers, and transactions from market participants. They assess the price at which a cargo could be bought or sold at the close of that window, applying a set of published criteria to determine which submissions are credible. The result is a single assessed price — the benchmark.

This structure has significant commercial implications. Because the benchmark is set in the last 30 minutes, large market participants can and do influence assessments by placing strategic bids or offers during the window. This is not illegal — it is how the market works — but it means a trader who understands the MOC process can read assessment-day positioning as a market signal in itself. Understanding **assessment timing**, the methodology differences between Platts and Argus, and how benchmarks like Dated Brent or JKM are constructed is essential for anyone working near the front office.

Price reporters don't just record what the market does — they assess what they believe a fair transaction would look like, based on available evidence. That distinction matters enormously when the market is thin and a small number of participants are setting the reference price for millions of barrels.

If you work in scheduling, analytics, risk, or trade finance, you will encounter Platts and Argus assessments constantly — in contract pricing, hedge references, and settlement calculations. Understanding how those prices are constructed helps you identify when an assessment may not reflect true market conditions — and when that discrepancy is a commercial risk or opportunity.
a.pullQuote: Price reporters don't just record what the market does — they assess what they believe a fair transaction would look like, based on available evidence. That distinction matters enormously when the market is thin and a small number of participants are setting the reference price for millions of barrels.

a.title: Risk Management on the Desk
a.desc: VaR, position limits, and how the desk manages market and credit exposure.
a.hook: Every trading desk operates inside a set of risk constraints it cannot breach. Understanding those constraints — how they are set, how they are monitored, and what happens when a position approaches a limit — is as important as understanding the trades themselves.
paragraphs: **Value at Risk (VaR)** is the most commonly used measure of market risk on a commodity trading desk. It estimates the maximum loss a portfolio of positions could suffer over a given time horizon at a given confidence level — typically 95% or 99% over a one-day or ten-day period. A VaR of $5 million at 95% confidence over one day means the desk should not expect to lose more than $5 million on more than 5% of trading days. VaR is used to set **position limits** — the maximum market exposure a trader or desk can carry — and is recalculated daily using current market data and the desk's live position.

Beyond VaR, desks manage several distinct risk types simultaneously. **Price risk** — the risk that flat price moves against the position — is the most obvious. **Basis risk** is the risk that the hedge and the physical position don't move together perfectly. **Credit risk** is the risk that a counterparty defaults before a trade settles. **Operational risk** covers vessel delays, cargo rejections, and documentation failures. **Liquidity risk** is the risk that a position cannot be exited at a reasonable price when needed.

Risk managers and traders interact daily on a commodity desk — and the relationship is not always comfortable. A risk manager's job is to enforce the limits and ask the questions a trader under P&L pressure might not want to answer. A trader's job is to take positions within those limits and explain their thesis clearly. When a position approaches a VaR limit, the risk manager can require the trader to reduce exposure — regardless of whether the trader believes the position is right. This separation of authority is what prevents single positions from becoming existential threats to the firm.

Risk management is not about preventing losses. It is about ensuring that no single loss, however bad, can threaten the desk's ability to keep trading. The limit exists so that being wrong once doesn't mean being out of business.

If you are targeting a risk, analytics, or middle-office role, this section is your starting point — but also read it if you are targeting a front-office role. Traders who understand the risk framework their desk operates within make better commercial decisions, because they know exactly how much latitude they have before the risk manager intervenes.
a.pullQuote: Risk management is not about preventing losses. It is about ensuring that no single loss, however bad, can threaten the desk's ability to keep trading. The limit exists so that being wrong once doesn't mean being out of business.

b.title: The Physical Trade Lifecycle
b.desc: From cargo enquiry to final settlement — every step a physical deal goes through.
b.hook: A physical commodity trade is not a single transaction. It is a chain of at least a dozen separate steps — each of which can go wrong, each of which has commercial and legal implications, and each of which requires a different function of the desk to execute correctly.
paragraphs: The lifecycle of a physical commodity deal begins with an **enquiry** — a buyer or seller reaches out to the market to test appetite. This is followed by negotiation of the commercial terms: volume, quality specification, price formula, loading port, delivery window, and payment terms. Once terms are agreed, a **confirmation** is exchanged — a legally binding document that records every agreed term. For large LNG deals this confirmation may be 20–30 pages; for spot crude trades it may be a one-page recap.

Once confirmed, the deal enters the **operations** phase. The scheduling team manages the vessel nomination, coordinates with the terminal for a loading slot, arranges the bill of lading and other shipping documents, and monitors the cargo in transit. For a DES trade, the seller owns and manages the vessel through to delivery; for an FOB trade, the buyer takes responsibility from the loading port. The operations team tracks the vessel via AIS and manages any changes to the delivery window.

Settlement occurs after delivery — the **final invoice** is calculated using the pricing formula in the confirmation, the cargo quantity is confirmed via an independent surveyor's report, and payment is made within the agreed credit terms (typically 30 days). The deal then flows into the back office for **P&L booking** in the ETRM system — connecting the physical trade to the hedge positions that were placed alongside it.

Every step of the trade lifecycle is a potential failure point. The front office closes the deal in an hour. Operations manages it for three weeks. The desk that ignores the operational layer will eventually have a very expensive surprise.

If you are targeting a scheduling, operations, or ETRM role, map every step of this lifecycle to the function that executes it — front office, middle office, back office, legal, and credit. Understanding where handoffs occur and what can go wrong at each one is what separates an effective operations professional from one who just processes paperwork.
b.pullQuote: Every step of the trade lifecycle is a potential failure point. The front office closes the deal in an hour. Operations manages it for three weeks. The desk that ignores the operational layer will eventually have a very expensive surprise.
b.handoff: Section B.2 covers the paper instruments that run alongside every physical deal — futures, swaps, and options that manage the price risk while the physical cargo is in transit.

b.title: Futures, Swaps & Options
b.desc: The paper instruments a desk uses alongside physical positions.
b.hook: Physical commodity traders are not just buying and selling cargoes. Every cargo they own carries a price risk that has to be managed — and the tools they use to manage it are futures, swaps, and options.
paragraphs: A **futures contract** is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a specific commodity at a specific price on a specific date. WTI crude futures on NYMEX and Brent futures on ICE are the most actively traded commodity futures contracts in the world. Futures are used by physical traders to hedge price exposure — if you own a cargo of crude, you sell futures to lock in the current price and remove the risk that the price falls before you sell the cargo.

A **swap** is an over-the-counter (OTC) contract where two parties exchange cash flows based on the difference between a floating price and a fixed price. Unlike futures, swaps are customised — they can reference any benchmark, any volume, any time period. For LNG traders, a JKM swap allows them to fix the price of a cargo that will be priced against the JKM assessment at delivery. Swaps are bilateral and carry counterparty credit risk; futures are exchange-cleared and carry no credit risk to the counterparty.

**Options** give the buyer the right — but not the obligation — to buy or sell a commodity at a specific price. A **cap** protects against price rising above a level; a **floor** protects against it falling below. Options cost a premium upfront but preserve upside. Physical traders use options when they want asymmetric protection — hedging downside risk while keeping the ability to benefit if the market moves in their favour.

The physical cargo is the position. The futures or swap is the hedge. The P&L lives in the difference between what you locked in on the paper and what you actually sell the physical for. Understanding that relationship is the entire job.

Even if you are not targeting a trading role, understanding these instruments is essential. Schedulers manage positions that are partially hedged. Risk managers monitor the hedge ratio. Analysts build the curve that prices the swaps. Every function on a commodity desk touches these instruments in some way.
b.pullQuote: The physical cargo is the position. The futures or swap is the hedge. The P&L lives in the difference between what you locked in on the paper and what you actually sell the physical for. Understanding that relationship is the entire job.
b.handoff: Section B.3 goes one level deeper — showing exactly how a physical position is hedged using paper instruments, and where the hedge can fail.

b.title: Hedging a Physical Position
b.desc: How a desk removes price risk from a cargo using paper markets.
b.hook: A hedge is not a bet in the opposite direction. It is a deliberate decision to remove price risk from a position — and the discipline of when to hedge, how much to hedge, and when not to hedge is one of the most important commercial skills on the desk.
paragraphs: When a physical trader buys a cargo of crude at $78/bbl, they immediately face the risk that the price will fall before they sell it. To remove that risk, they sell futures or swaps at the same price — creating a **hedge**. If crude falls to $74/bbl, the physical cargo loses $4/bbl, but the short futures position gains $4/bbl. The losses and gains offset — the desk is flat the market. If crude rises to $82/bbl, the physical cargo gains $4/bbl but the futures position loses $4/bbl. Again, flat the market.

In practice, hedges are rarely perfect. **Basis risk** is the risk that the physical price and the futures price do not move together exactly. A cargo of West African crude priced against Dated Brent may be hedged with ICE Brent futures — but if the Brent-WA differential widens, the hedge loses effectiveness. The desk is still exposed to the differential move even though it thought it was hedged. Managing basis risk is a significant part of day-to-day risk management.

The decision of **how much to hedge** — the hedge ratio — is both commercial and strategic. A 100% hedge removes all price risk but also all upside. A 50% hedge retains some exposure to the market's direction. Some desks have mandatory hedge ratios enforced by risk policy; others allow trader discretion. The choice depends on the firm's risk appetite, the desk's P&L mandate, and the trader's confidence in their market view.

Being perfectly hedged means being perfectly wrong — you gave away all your upside to remove your downside. The art is knowing how much risk you actually need to carry to generate the return the business requires.

Every time you see a commodity firm report a trading loss, the question to ask is not 'why did the price go against them?' but 'why wasn't the position hedged?' The answer usually involves one of three things: deliberate directional exposure, basis risk that wasn't accounted for, or a hedge that worked in theory but couldn't be executed in the market at the assumed rate.
b.pullQuote: Being perfectly hedged means being perfectly wrong — you gave away all your upside to remove your downside. The art is knowing how much risk you actually need to carry to generate the return the business requires.

b.title: Basis & the Differential
b.desc: Why the same commodity trades at different prices in different places.
b.hook: Dubai crude is not Brent crude. Dated Brent is not ICE Brent futures. HSFO in Singapore is not HSFO in Rotterdam. Every commodity trades at a spread to every benchmark — and understanding that spread is what separates a physical trader from a paper one.
paragraphs: **Basis** is the difference between the physical commodity price and the benchmark futures price. For a US Gulf Coast refiner buying domestic crude, the basis is the difference between the wellhead price of a specific crude grade and WTI futures. Basis reflects the cost of transportation to the delivery point of the futures contract, quality differences between the physical grade and the benchmark grade, and any supply/demand imbalances specific to that location.

In practice, traders talk about **differentials** — the premium or discount at which a physical commodity trades relative to a benchmark. Dubai crude trades at a differential to Brent. West African Bonny Light trades at a premium to Dated Brent because of its lower sulphur content and higher gasoline yield. Russian Urals trades at a discount because it is heavier and higher in sulphur. These differentials move constantly based on refinery demand, freight rates, and regional supply dynamics.

Basis risk arises when a hedge is placed using a benchmark that does not perfectly track the physical commodity being hedged. A Singapore gasoil trader who hedges a physical gasoil cargo with ICE gasoil futures is exposed to the Singapore-Rotterdam gasoil differential — the basis. If Singapore gasoil weakens relative to Rotterdam, the physical cargo loses value even though the futures hedge holds. Basis risk is real, difficult to eliminate entirely, and the source of many trading losses that are mistakenly attributed to 'being wrong on the market'.

Traders lose money on basis all the time while being right on flat price. You can nail the direction of Brent perfectly and still lose money on a West African cargo if you didn't account for the differential move.

When you are reading about commodity price differentials in the news — Urals at a discount to Brent, JKM premium to TTF narrowing — you are reading about basis. Understanding what drives those differentials (quality, freight, regional supply, sanctions) is what connects the financial market to the physical one.
b.pullQuote: Traders lose money on basis all the time while being right on flat price. You can nail the direction of Brent perfectly and still lose money on a West African cargo if you didn't account for the differential move.
b.handoff: Section B.5 covers the EFS — the mechanism that physically connects the paper and physical markets and allows a desk to move exposure from one to the other.

b.title: The Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS)
b.desc: How traders move between physical and paper positions.
b.hook: The EFS is one of the least-discussed mechanisms in commodity markets — and one of the most important for understanding how physical and paper markets stay connected to each other.
paragraphs: An **Exchange of Futures for Swaps (EFS)** is a privately negotiated transaction in which one party exchanges a futures position for an OTC swap position. The exchange takes place at an agreed price and is then registered with the exchange. The result is that one party ends up with a futures contract and the other ends up with a swap — each has moved from one instrument to the other without entering the open market.

EFS transactions are used when a trader wants to move from a standardised exchange-traded position to a customised OTC position — or vice versa. For example, a physical LNG trader who has hedged a cargo with JKM futures may want to convert that hedge into a JKM swap with a different settlement date to better match the physical cargo's pricing period. The EFS allows this conversion without the market impact of unwinding the futures position and placing a new swap separately.

EFS activity is a useful market intelligence signal. High EFS volume in a specific commodity and tenor suggests that physical market participants are actively adjusting their hedge positions — often because physical market conditions are changing. When a large volume of crude futures is exchanged into longer-dated swaps, it may signal that desks are repositioning for a change in the forward curve structure.
Every time the physical and paper markets seem to be telling different stories, look at the EFS volume. It's often where traders are quietly moving their positions from one world to the other.

For most students and career switchers, the EFS is a concept to understand rather than a mechanism to operate. Knowing what it is and why it exists helps you understand how the physical and paper markets remain connected — and how large desks manage their positions across both simultaneously.
b.pullQuote: Every time the physical and paper markets seem to be telling different stories, look at the EFS volume. It's often where traders are quietly moving their positions from one world to the other.
b.handoff: Section B.6 covers options — the instruments that give a desk asymmetric exposure: protection on the downside with the ability to benefit from upside.

b.title: Options in Commodity Markets
b.desc: Caps, floors, collars — how optionality is priced and used.
b.hook: Options give you the right to act without the obligation. In commodity markets, that asymmetry — protecting against the bad outcome while keeping the good one — has real and measurable value.
paragraphs: A commodity **call option** gives the buyer the right to purchase a commodity at a fixed price (the **strike price**) before a specific date. A **put option** gives the right to sell at the strike price. The buyer pays a **premium** upfront for this right. If the market moves in the buyer's favour, they exercise the option and benefit. If the market moves against them, they let the option expire and only lose the premium — unlike a futures contract, where losses are uncapped.

In commodity markets, options are used in several common structures. A **cap** is a call option that protects a buyer against prices rising above a level — used by utilities and airlines to fix their maximum fuel cost. A **floor** is a put option that protects a seller against prices falling below a level — used by producers to guarantee a minimum revenue. A **collar** combines a cap and a floor — the buyer gives up some upside in exchange for paying a lower premium, or no premium at all if the collar is costless.

Option pricing is driven primarily by **implied volatility** — the market's expectation of how much the underlying commodity price will move. High volatility means options are expensive because the probability of the option being in-the-money is higher. Physical commodity traders watch implied volatility as a market signal: a sudden spike in crude option volatility often precedes or accompanies a significant physical market event — a supply disruption, an OPEC announcement, or a demand shock.
The premium you pay for an option is the price of sleeping well at night. The question is whether the cost of that peace of mind is justified by the risk you're actually carrying.

Options are used extensively in trade finance and hedging structures for commodity deals — particularly long-term LNG offtake agreements and producer hedging programmes. Understanding the basic mechanics — what a cap and floor do, what affects the premium, how optionality in a physical contract has measurable value — gives you a significant edge in analytical and structuring roles.
b.pullQuote: The premium you pay for an option is the price of sleeping well at night. The question is whether the cost of that peace of mind is justified by the risk you're actually carrying.

b.title: Term Contracts vs. Spot Trading
b.desc: The commercial logic behind long-term offtake and spot market exposure.
b.hook: A commodity desk that trades only spot is taking maximum market exposure. One that trades only on long-term contracts is leaving significant upside on the table. The mix between term and spot is one of the most consequential strategic decisions a commodity firm makes.
paragraphs: A **term contract** is a multi-year supply agreement between a producer and a buyer — typically at a price linked to a benchmark with an agreed formula. LNG term contracts are the clearest example: a Japanese utility might sign a 20-year contract with an Australian LNG producer, with volume and price formula agreed upfront. Term contracts provide certainty for both parties — the producer finances the investment, the buyer secures supply. But they also remove the ability to benefit from spot market moves.

The **spot market** is where uncontracted volumes trade — cargo by cargo, at the current market price. Trading firms active in the spot market can capture arbitrage opportunities, respond to supply disruptions, and earn from volatility in ways that term-contract buyers cannot. But they also face the risk that spot prices move sharply against them, and they must continuously source supply and place cargoes without the certainty of contracted volumes.

Most large commodity traders and energy companies run a **portfolio approach** — anchoring their book with enough term contracts to guarantee base supply and revenue, then trading the margin on the spot market. The optimal ratio between term and spot exposure depends on the firm's risk tolerance, the volatility of the underlying commodity, and the desk's ability to manage spot market positions actively. A common structure for LNG is 70–80% term, 20–30% spot — but this shifts significantly during periods of high market volatility.
A term contract is certainty. A spot position is optionality. Most commodity firms need both — and the firms that manage the balance best are the ones that consistently outperform their peers.

If you are targeting an origination or commercial role, understanding the term vs. spot trade-off is central to how you will structure deals and advise clients. If you are targeting an analytics or scheduling role, understanding this distinction explains why some cargo programmes are fixed and others are dynamic — and why your scheduling flexibility changes depending on the contract type.
b.pullQuote: A term contract is certainty. A spot position is optionality. Most commodity firms need both — and the firms that manage the balance best are the ones that consistently outperform their peers.
b.handoff: Section B.8 shows how all of these positions — physical cargoes, futures hedges, swap exposures, term contracts, and spot trades — stack up together in a trading book.

b.title: The Trading Book — How Positions Stack Up
b.desc: How a desk tracks its combined physical, paper, and freight exposure.
b.hook: At any given moment, a commodity trading desk has dozens of positions simultaneously — physical cargoes on the water, futures hedges on the exchange, OTC swaps with counterparties, freight fixtures, and term contract obligations. The trading book is how the desk sees all of them at once.
paragraphs: The **trading book** is the consolidated view of all open positions on the desk — physical and paper, long and short, hedged and unhedged. It is maintained in an **ETRM system** (Energy Trading and Risk Management platform) — typically Endur, RightAngle, or Allegro — which books every trade, marks positions to market daily, calculates P&L, and feeds risk metrics to the risk management function.

A well-structured trading book shows, for every commodity and time period: the net physical long or short position (how many barrels or MMBtu the desk owns or owes), the hedge position (the offsetting paper contracts), the net unhedged exposure (the **open position**), and the current mark-to-market P&L on each leg. Traders review their book every morning before markets open — checking overnight price moves, assessing whether any positions need to be adjusted, and planning the day's trading activity.

The interaction between physical and paper positions in the book creates a number of important metrics that risk managers monitor daily. **Hedge effectiveness** — what percentage of the physical exposure is covered by paper hedges. **Greeks** — for options positions, the sensitivity of the position value to price changes (delta), volatility changes (vega), and time decay (theta). And **roll risk** — the risk that a paper position approaching expiry cannot be rolled forward at an acceptable price.

The trading book is the desk's truth. A trader's P&L is not what they think they've made — it's what the book says, marked to today's market prices, with every position they actually have, not the ones they wish they had.

ETRM system knowledge is explicitly valued in almost every commodity trading job description outside the front office. Understanding what a trading book is, what goes into it, and how positions are marked to market gives you the context to add value in scheduling, analytics, risk, finance, or technology roles — not just trading.
b.pullQuote: The trading book is the desk's truth. A trader's P&L is not what they think they've made — it's what the book says, marked to today's market prices, with every position they actually have, not the ones they wish they had.

c.title: Vessel Classes & What They Carry
c.desc: VLCCs, Suezmax, Aframax, LNG carriers — what each class moves and why it matters.
c.hook: The vessel class determines what trade is even possible. A VLCC cannot enter most Asian import terminals. An Aframax cannot make the Middle East Gulf–Far East route economical. Before any arbitrage calc, the desk asks: what vessel can actually do this voyage?
paragraphs: The tanker market is segmented by vessel size, each class defined by its carrying capacity and the routes and terminals it can access. A **VLCC** (Very Large Crude Carrier) carries 1.8–2.2 million barrels of crude and is the workhouse of long-haul crude trades — Middle East Gulf to Asia, West Africa to the US, and North Sea to Asia. Its scale makes it the most cost-effective vessel for high-volume, long-distance routes, but its draft restricts access to many ports.

A **Suezmax** carries around 1 million barrels — sized to transit the Suez Canal loaded. It is used on routes where a VLCC cannot access the port or where cargo sizes are smaller. An **Aframax** carries 500,000–750,000 barrels and is the dominant vessel in the Baltic, the Mediterranean, and cross-Caribbean trades. A **Panamax** is sized to transit the Panama Canal — important for US Gulf to Asia routes.

LNG carriers are a completely different category — purpose-built, double-hulled, and insulated to maintain cargo at -162°C. They range from 125,000 m³ to 210,000 m³ (Q-Flex and Q-Max classes for Qatar). The specialised nature of LNG carriers means the fleet is much smaller than the crude tanker fleet, and vessel availability is a genuine constraint on LNG trade volumes. LNG carrier hire rates are quoted in $/day and tracked via the Baltic Exchange LNG Carrier Index.

The vessel class is not just a logistics detail. It determines which routes are viable, which terminals can receive the cargo, and ultimately which arbitrages are executable. The desk that doesn't know its vessel classes doesn't know its market.

In a scheduling or operations role, vessel class knowledge is non-negotiable. In a trading or analytics role, understanding which vessel type is needed for a specific route tells you immediately which freight index to track and what the realistic freight cost assumption is for any trade you are evaluating.
c.pullQuote: The vessel class is not just a logistics detail. It determines which routes are viable, which terminals can receive the cargo, and ultimately which arbitrages are executable. The desk that doesn't know its vessel classes doesn't know its market.
c.handoff: Section C.2 covers how the freight rates for those vessels are set — the Baltic Exchange, spot fixtures, and the market mechanics that drive the cost of every cargo movement.

c.title: How Freight Rates Are Set
c.desc: The Baltic Exchange indices, spot fixtures, and time charter markets.
c.hook: Freight rates can double in a week or halve in a month. Understanding what drives that volatility — and being positioned to act on it before the rest of the market — is a genuine commercial edge on any commodity desk.
paragraphs: Freight rates for crude tankers are quoted in **Worldscale** points — a percentage of a published standard rate that accounts for vessel size, route distance, and standard costs. WS100 is the flat rate; WS120 means 20% above flat, WS80 means 20% below. The Baltic Exchange publishes indices for each vessel class: the **BDTI** (Baltic Dirty Tanker Index) aggregates routes for crude tankers, the BCTI for clean product tankers, and the BLNG for LNG carriers. These indices are reported daily and are the standard reference for freight market activity.

The spot freight market is where voyage charters are fixed — a specific vessel hired for a specific voyage at an agreed rate. The rate is set by negotiation between the shipowner or broker and the charterer, reflecting current vessel availability on the relevant route, cargo size, port conditions, and overall market sentiment. When many cargoes are seeking vessels simultaneously — for example, at the start of a new OPEC production cycle — rates spike. When vessel supply exceeds cargo demand, rates collapse.

The **time charter market** is where vessels are hired for a period — 6 months, 1 year, 3 years — at a fixed daily rate. A charterer paying $35,000/day for a VLCC on a 12-month time charter is betting that spot freight rates will average above that level during the period. Time charters provide certainty of vessel access and protection against freight rate spikes — but at a cost premium over spot if rates remain low.

Freight is a commodity in its own right — it has its own supply and demand balance, its own seasonal patterns, and its own arbitrage signals. The desk that treats freight as just a cost has already given away part of its edge.

Freight rate literacy is useful in every function near the commodity desk. For schedulers, it informs vessel selection and charter decisions. For analysts, it is a key input to any arbitrage or P&L model. For traders, it is a variable that can be traded — not just assumed.
c.pullQuote: Freight is a commodity in its own right — it has its own supply and demand balance, its own seasonal patterns, and its own arbitrage signals. The desk that treats freight as just a cost has already given away part of its edge.
c.handoff: Section C.3 covers what happens once the vessel is fixed — the port operations, laytime mechanics, and demurrage costs that determine whether the voyage stays within budget.

c.title: Laytime, Demurrage & Port Economics
c.desc: Why every hour in port costs money — and how it's calculated.
c.hook: Demurrage is one of the most contested financial items in commodity trading — and one of the most avoidable. A 2-day delay at a terminal on a VLCC can cost $80,000 or more. Most of it is preventable with better operations.
paragraphs: **Laytime** is the number of hours agreed in the charter party within which the charterer must complete loading or discharging the cargo. It begins once the vessel has arrived at the port, tendered its **Notice of Readiness (NOR)**, and is cleared to proceed to berth. If loading is completed within the allowed laytime, no additional payment is required. If it takes longer, the charterer pays **demurrage** — the daily rate specified in the charter party — for every hour of delay.

Demurrage rates for VLCCs typically run $25,000–$60,000 per day. Aframax rates are lower, typically $15,000–$30,000 per day. LNG carrier demurrage is higher — often $60,000–$100,000 per day for a modern Q-Flex. Demurrage claims are a regular feature of physical commodity trading — when multiple vessels arrive at the same terminal at the same time, berth queues form and laytime runs. Terminal operators, loading masters, and port agents all play roles in managing the clock. If loading completes early, **dispatch** — the reverse of demurrage — may be owed to the charterer by the shipowner.

**Laytime calculations** are governed by specific clause language in the charter party — which events start and stop the clock, how weather delays are treated, how weekend and holiday time is counted. Even seemingly small differences in clause language — 'SHEX' (Sundays and Holidays Excepted) vs. 'SHINC' (Sundays and Holidays Included) — can have significant financial implications on a slow-loading cargo. Demurrage disputes are common and are often resolved through negotiation or arbitration.

Demurrage is the penalty for poor coordination. It is almost always preventable — but it requires the terminal, the vessel, the loader, and the receiver to all be in sync. When they're not, someone pays for it. In most charter parties, that someone is the charterer.

If you are targeting a scheduling or operations role, laytime and demurrage are non-negotiable knowledge. If you are in an analytical or commercial role, understanding demurrage helps you evaluate the true operational cost of a trade beyond the freight rate — and identify where poorly managed operations are eating into trading P&L.
c.pullQuote: Demurrage is the penalty for poor coordination. It is almost always preventable — but it requires the terminal, the vessel, the loader, and the receiver to all be in sync. When they're not, someone pays for it. In most charter parties, that someone is the charterer.
c.handoff: Section C.4 looks at the nomination process — how physical liftings are coordinated between buyer, seller, vessel, and terminal before a single barrel moves.

c.title: Cargo Nominations & Scheduling
c.desc: How physical liftings are coordinated between buyer, seller, and vessel.
c.hook: A cargo nomination is where the commercial deal and the physical world meet. Get it wrong — miss a window, nominate the wrong vessel, submit late — and you are in breach of contract. Get it right, consistently, at scale, and you are running an elite operations function.
paragraphs: Once a physical commodity deal is confirmed, the operations process begins with a **nomination**. The buyer nominates a vessel by submitting the vessel's details — name, flag, deadweight, age, class — to the seller within the timeframe specified in the contract. The seller has the right to reject a vessel that does not meet the contractual specifications — too old, wrong flag, unacceptable insurer. Once the vessel is accepted, the **loading window** (or laycan) is agreed — typically a range of dates within which the vessel must arrive at the loading port.

A **cargo programme** is the schedule of all liftings for a given production facility or terminal over a month or quarter. For an LNG liquefaction plant exporting 20+ cargoes per month, the cargo programme must balance vessel availability, terminal constraints, buyer obligations, and maintenance windows simultaneously. Scheduling teams manage this programme continuously — adjusting for vessel delays, terminal downtime, and changes in buyer demand. A well-run cargo programme maximises throughput and minimises demurrage; a poorly-run one generates losses, disputes, and damaged counterparty relationships.

When a cargo must be adjusted — loading date shifted, volume changed, vessel substituted — both parties must agree to the variation. These variations are negotiated between the operations and scheduling teams, often under time pressure, and require documenting formally to avoid disputes at settlement. For term contracts with complex flexibility provisions, the scheduling process can involve dozens of communication touches per cargo.

Scheduling is where commercial decisions become physical reality. A trader can close a deal in an hour. The scheduling team lives with it for 30 days — managing every variation, every delay, every dispute until the cargo is delivered and the invoice is settled.

Scheduling and operations roles are consistently undervalued as entry points into commodity trading — but they offer the fastest route to deep operational knowledge of how physical markets actually work. Every trader who came up through operations understands the commercial implications of execution risk in a way that desk-only analysts often don't.
c.pullQuote: Scheduling is where commercial decisions become physical reality. A trader can close a deal in an hour. The scheduling team lives with it for 30 days — managing every variation, every delay, every dispute until the cargo is delivered and the invoice is settled.
c.handoff: Section C.5 covers AIS tracking — the technology layer that gives desks real-time visibility into where every vessel is, what it is carrying, and what that movement means for market supply and demand.

c.title: AIS Tracking & Real-Time Flow Data
c.desc: Using vessel position data as a market intelligence signal.
c.hook: Every commercial vessel on the ocean broadcasts its position, speed, and destination every few seconds. That data is available to anyone. The traders who know how to read it see supply disruptions, cargo diversions, and market shifts before they show up in any price report.
paragraphs: **AIS** (Automatic Identification System) is a maritime tracking system required on all commercial vessels over 300 gross tonnes. Each vessel broadcasts its position, speed, heading, destination, and cargo status continuously via radio signal and satellite relay. Platforms like Kpler, Vortexa, MarineTraffic, and Bloomberg's vessel tracking tools aggregate this data and present it in real time — showing where every LNG carrier, VLCC, and Aframax is, where it is heading, and what it is carrying.

Commodity trading desks use AIS data as a real-time market intelligence tool. If an LNG carrier deviates significantly from its filed route — turning north toward Europe when its destination was logged as Japan — that is a cargo diversion signal. The desk can see it via AIS before any market report covers it, giving a window to act on the supply implication before the price adjusts. Similarly, a cluster of loaded VLCCs anchoring off Singapore signals floating storage is building — a bearish indicator for crude that shows up in AIS data days before it appears in official inventory statistics.

Platforms like **Kpler** and **Vortexa** go beyond raw AIS tracking — they use machine learning to infer cargo grades, volumes, and trade flows from vessel movements and port call patterns. This allows desks to estimate LNG exports from a specific liquefaction plant, track crude flows from a sanctioned country, or monitor the build-up of product supply in a regional hub — all from vessel movement data, without relying on official reporting.

By the time the EIA report comes out, the smart money already knows what's in it — because they've been watching the vessels for two weeks. AIS data is the physical market's live signal. Price is the lagging indicator.

AIS platform literacy — knowing how to use Kpler or Vortexa to answer a specific market question — is an increasingly valued skill in commodity analytics and intelligence roles. Even a basic ability to interpret vessel tracking data puts you ahead of the vast majority of candidates entering the industry.
c.pullQuote: By the time the EIA report comes out, the smart money already knows what's in it — because they've been watching the vessels for two weeks. AIS data is the physical market's live signal. Price is the lagging indicator.
c.handoff: Section C.6 brings AIS intelligence and freight economics together in the cargo diversion decision — the moment when all of this information must be synthesised into a real-time commercial call.

c.title: The Cargo Diversion Decision
c.desc: When and why a vessel changes destination mid-voyage — and the economics behind it.
c.hook: A cargo diversion is the physical commodity market's fastest response mechanism to a price signal. When a spread opens wide enough to cover freight and risk, a vessel mid-voyage can change destination in hours. The desk that moves first captures the margin; the desk that moves second finds the window has already closed.
paragraphs: A **cargo diversion** occurs when a vessel changes its destination mid-voyage — typically because a price differential between the original destination and an alternative has widened enough to make rerouting profitable after accounting for all additional costs. The decision involves the cargo owner, the vessel operator, and often the original cargo buyer — who must agree to release the cargo or accept a price adjustment.

The economics of a diversion are calculated in real time. The desk must quantify: the gross price differential between the two destinations, the additional freight cost of the longer or different route, any canal or port cost changes, the additional voyage time and its carrying cost, the contractual flexibility provisions that allow diversion, and the counterparty credit of the new buyer. All of this must be resolved — often in hours — before another desk spots the same opportunity and the spread begins to close.

The **DES vs. FOB distinction** is critical for diversions. Under a DES (Delivered Ex-Ship) contract, the seller controls the vessel and can make the diversion decision unilaterally — subject to the terms of the original sale contract. Under an FOB contract, the buyer owns the vessel from the loading port and makes the diversion decision. Understanding which party controls the vessel determines who captures the diversion P&L and who needs to negotiate a release.

The cargo diversion window is measured in hours, not days. By the time a market report confirms the arbitrage is open, the fastest desks have already fixed the vessels. Speed and preparation are more valuable than analysis after the fact.

The cargo diversion is the most commercially intensive moment in physical commodity trading — requiring real-time integration of freight, pricing, operations, legal, and credit inputs. For students and career changers, understanding the decision logic end-to-end is one of the clearest signals of commercial awareness you can demonstrate in an interview.
c.pullQuote: The cargo diversion window is measured in hours, not days. By the time a market report confirms the arbitrage is open, the fastest desks have already fixed the vessels. Speed and preparation are more valuable than analysis after the fact.
c.handoff: Section C.7 moves to the documentation layer — the bills of lading, letters of indemnity, and certificates that make a physical commodity trade legally real.

c.title: Trade Documentation & Operations
c.desc: Bills of lading, LOIs, and the paperwork that makes a physical trade real.
c.hook: A commodity trade is not complete until the documentation is right. The cargo on the vessel is worth nothing until the bill of lading is issued. And a bill of lading issued with incorrect information can create a commercial and legal crisis that takes months to resolve.
paragraphs: The **bill of lading (BL)** is the central document in every physical commodity trade. It serves three functions simultaneously: it is evidence of the contract of carriage between shipper and carrier; it is a receipt for the cargo showing quantity and condition at loading; and it is a document of title — whoever holds the original bill of lading has legal title to the cargo. BLs are issued in three originals; to take delivery of the cargo, the receiver must surrender an original BL at the discharge port.

When a cargo is traded before the BL can be physically transferred to the new buyer — which is common in rapidly-moving spot markets — the parties use a **Letter of Indemnity (LOI)**. The LOI allows the receiver to take delivery without presenting the original BL, in exchange for the seller's indemnity against any loss that results. LOIs are common but carry risk — if the underlying trade goes wrong, the indemnity can be called upon. Many banks and sophisticated counterparties limit their LOI exposure carefully.

Additional key documents include the **Certificate of Quality (CoQ)** — the independent inspector's analysis of the cargo's physical properties (API gravity, sulphur content, water content, etc.) — and the **Certificate of Quantity (CQ)** — the volume delivered, measured by an independent surveyor. Both certificates are used to calculate the final invoice and are the basis for any quality or quantity claims.

The paperwork is not admin. It is the legal and financial infrastructure of the trade. A BL issued with the wrong quantity, a missing CoQ, or an LOI from an uncredited counterparty can cost more to resolve than the cargo was worth.

Document management is handled by the back office in most large firms, but understanding what each document represents — and what can go wrong when documentation is incomplete or incorrect — is essential for anyone working in scheduling, operations, trade finance, or legal roles in commodity trading.
c.pullQuote: The paperwork is not admin. It is the legal and financial infrastructure of the trade. A BL issued with the wrong quantity, a missing CoQ, or an LOI from an uncredited counterparty can cost more to resolve than the cargo was worth.

c.title: Freight as a Revenue Source
c.desc: How desks generate P&L from freight positions, not just from commodity price.
c.hook: The most sophisticated commodity trading desks do not just manage freight as a cost. They take freight positions — locking in vessel economics before the market moves — and earn from the differential between what they pay and what the market moves to.
paragraphs: A commodity desk that secures freight at a rate below the market level earns a **freight premium** — the difference between the cheap fixture and the current market rate. This can be achieved by fixing vessels early, before a seasonal demand surge, or by locking in time charters at rates that prove below the subsequent spot market. The desk that locks in a VLCC at $35,000/day in January and watches spot rates move to $55,000/day by March has effectively earned $20,000/day on that vessel — even before the commodity cargo is loaded.

**Forward Freight Agreements (FFAs)** are financial derivatives that allow a desk to take a position on future freight rates without owning or hiring a vessel. An FFA is a contract to pay or receive the difference between a fixed rate and the actual Baltic Exchange route rate on a future date. A desk that sells FFAs at $45,000/day and watches spot rates fall to $35,000/day earns $10,000/day on the paper position. FFAs are used both to hedge existing freight exposure and to take directional views on freight rates as a standalone trade.

The interaction between commodity price and freight creates complex P&L dynamics. Rising commodity prices increase the value of cargoes already on the water; rising freight rates increase the cost of moving them. A desk that is long physical cargo and short freight (via FFAs) profits from the commodity rise but hedges the freight cost increase. The ability to manage both legs simultaneously — commodity and freight — is one of the distinguishing capabilities of the largest commodity trading firms.

Freight is not a tax on trade. It is a market with its own supply and demand balance, its own seasonality, and its own arbitrage signals. The desk that figures this out generates revenue from two markets simultaneously instead of one.

For analysts and structurers, freight as a P&L source means that any commodity trade model that treats freight as a fixed cost input is incomplete. The sensitivity of the overall trade P&L to freight rate movements — and the options available to hedge or monetise that sensitivity — should be part of every trade analysis.
c.pullQuote: Freight is not a tax on trade. It is a market with its own supply and demand balance, its own seasonality, and its own arbitrage signals. The desk that figures this out generates revenue from two markets simultaneously instead of one.

d.title: How a Trader Forms a Market View
d.desc: The information sources, signals, and reasoning process behind a position.
d.hook: A market view is not a prediction. It is a structured argument — built from data, tested against the physical market, and held with enough conviction to put real money behind it while remaining open enough to change when the evidence changes.
paragraphs: A commodity trader's market view is built from multiple information layers, each of which contributes a different piece of the picture. The **fundamental layer** covers supply and demand: production rates, refinery runs, LNG liquefaction capacity, inventory levels, seasonal demand patterns. The **flow layer** covers physical movement: vessel positions, port congestion, cargo flows from AIS data. The **positioning layer** covers what other market participants are doing: speculative positioning from COT data, physical buying interest from broker activity.

The art of forming a view is knowing which layer is dominant in the current market environment. In a supply disruption, fundamentals dominate — the physical availability of cargo is the primary driver. In a quiet, balanced market, positioning often dominates — speculative flows and option hedging mechanics drive more price movement than fundamental changes. A trader who applies the wrong lens to the current market environment will consistently misread the signals.

Once a view is formed, the trader must assess its **conviction level** and size the position accordingly. A high-conviction view — where the fundamental thesis is clear, the timing is supported by technical signals, and the risk/reward is attractive — justifies a full position. A low-conviction view — where the thesis is plausible but the timing is uncertain — might justify a smaller position or no position at all. The discipline of sizing positions in proportion to conviction, and not in proportion to the desire to make money, is one of the hardest skills to develop.

A good view is not one that turns out to be right. A good view is one that is well-reasoned, properly sized, and held with the right conviction level for the available evidence. Being right for bad reasons is as dangerous as being wrong.

Market view formation is not just a front-office skill. Analytics professionals build the data infrastructure that supports view formation. Risk managers challenge the conviction level of views being translated into positions. Schedulers implement the operational consequences of views. Understanding the process of forming a market view helps every function around the desk do its job better.
d.pullQuote: A good view is not one that turns out to be right. A good view is one that is well-reasoned, properly sized, and held with the right conviction level for the available evidence. Being right for bad reasons is as dangerous as being wrong.
d.handoff: Section D.2 goes into the most widely watched weekly fundamental signal — the EIA petroleum status report — and shows how the desk actually reads it.

d.title: Reading the EIA Report
d.desc: The weekly inventory release — what it contains and what the desk looks for.
d.hook: The EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report is released every Wednesday at 10:30am Eastern Time. For the next 90 seconds, nothing else matters in the crude oil market. What the desk does in those 90 seconds — and in the two weeks of data preparation before them — is what separates an informed trader from one who reads headlines.
paragraphs: The EIA report covers the previous week's US petroleum data — crude oil stocks, gasoline stocks, distillate stocks, total petroleum stocks, refinery inputs, refinery utilisation rates, crude imports, crude production, and product demand implied by deliveries. The headline number markets focus on first is the **crude inventory change** — the week-on-week build or draw in commercial crude stocks. But experienced traders look beyond the headline immediately.

The desk compares the actual number to two benchmarks: the **analyst consensus** (the average estimate from a survey of market analysts published by Reuters or Bloomberg the day before), and the **5-year seasonal average** for that week. A 3 million barrel draw sounds bullish in isolation — but if the consensus was expecting a 5 million barrel draw, the actual number is bearish relative to expectations. And if the 5-year average for that week shows a seasonal draw of 4 million barrels, the actual is also below seasonal norms. Both comparisons together give the real signal.

Beyond crude, the desk analyses the product split — what happened to gasoline and distillate stocks, and whether the changes are consistent with the crude number. A crude draw with a gasoline build might indicate refinery throughput increased but demand didn't absorb the output — a less bullish signal than a crude draw with product draws across the board. The report also shows **days of forward supply** — how many days of current consumption the existing stock represents — which contextualises the absolute inventory level.

The number that matters is not the crude draw — it is the crude draw minus the expectation, adjusted for what the seasonal average says should be happening. Only then do you know whether the market is actually tighter or looser than people thought.

EIA literacy is one of the most immediately applicable skills you can develop before entering the industry. The report is free, weekly, and publicly available at eia.gov. Reading it for 12 consecutive weeks — tracking the actual vs. consensus delta and noting what the market does in response — will teach you more about how physical oil markets work than most university courses.
d.pullQuote: The number that matters is not the crude draw — it is the crude draw minus the expectation, adjusted for what the seasonal average says should be happening. Only then do you know whether the market is actually tighter or looser than people thought.
