d.title: The Forward Curve — Structure & Signals
d.desc: Contango, backwardation, and what the curve shape tells the desk about physical supply balance.
d.hook: The forward curve is the commodity market's continuous opinion poll on the future. Its shape — sloping up, sloping down, or humped — tells you something important about the current physical balance of the market that no single data point can match.
paragraphs: The **forward curve** plots the prices at which a commodity can be bought or sold for delivery at different future dates. When front-month prices are lower than deferred prices — the curve slopes upward — the market is in **contango**. When front-month prices are higher than deferred prices, the market is in **backwardation**. These two states reflect fundamentally different physical market conditions and call for different commercial responses.

Contango signals oversupply or weak near-term demand. The gap between spot and forward prices creates an incentive to buy the cheap spot commodity, store it, and sell it forward at the higher price — the **carry trade**. The spread must be large enough to cover storage costs, insurance, financing, and the cost of tying up capital. When the carry trade is profitable, inventories build as storage is filled. This additional physical demand from storage gradually narrows the contango — it is self-limiting.

Backwardation signals tight physical supply or strong near-term demand. Buyers are willing to pay a premium for prompt delivery over future delivery because they need the commodity now — not in three months. Storage is uneconomic in backwardation because the opportunity cost of holding inventory is high. Refiners draw down stocks, floating storage is released, and the prompt market tightens further. Backwardation tends to persist until new supply arrives or demand softens — at which point the curve flips back toward flat or contango.
The curve shape tells you more than any headline. Before you read a news story, look at where M1 is trading versus M6. The market already knows — it is telling you in the structure.

The forward curve is published daily for every major commodity. Learning to read it — identifying whether it is in contango or backwardation, how steeply, and whether the structure is changing — is one of the most immediately applicable market skills you can develop. Bloomberg, ICE, and CME all provide forward curve data; many free platforms show at least the front three or four months.
d.pullQuote: The curve shape tells you more than any headline. Before you read a news story, look at where M1 is trading versus M6. The market already knows — it is telling you in the structure.
d.handoff: Section D.4 explains how the prices that populate that forward curve are actually assessed and published — the price reporting agency methodology.

d.title: Price Assessment Methodology
d.desc: How Platts, Argus, and ICIS assess physical commodity prices.
d.hook: The price assessments published by Platts and Argus are referenced in contracts covering billions of dollars of commodity supply. Understanding how those assessments are produced is not just academic — it is a commercial skill that affects how you negotiate, hedge, and settle trades.
paragraphs: The dominant price reporting methodology for crude oil and refined products is **Market on Close (MOC)**, developed by Platts. During the final 30 minutes of the trading day — the assessment window — reporters collect bids, offers, and completed transactions from market participants via a regulated platform. They apply a published set of criteria to assess which submissions are credible and calculate the benchmark price at the close of the window. The resulting assessment — Dated Brent, HSFO 380 Singapore, Singapore Gasoil — becomes the reference price for physical contracts and financial derivatives linked to it.

Argus uses a similar but distinct methodology — its assessments are typically based on reported transactions during the trading day rather than a specific close-of-day window. This means Argus and Platts assessments for the same commodity can diverge slightly, particularly in thin or fast-moving markets. Physical contracts will specify which agency's assessment applies — and switching from one to the other can have significant commercial implications, as the two assessments sometimes move differently.

Market participants are aware that the MOC window can be influenced by strategic participation — placing large bids or offers to push the assessment in a direction that benefits existing positions. This is legal within the framework of the methodology, but regulated. The UK's FCA, the US CFTC, and the EU's REMIT regime all monitor assessment window activity. Understanding the boundary between legitimate market participation and manipulation is a compliance-critical topic for anyone working near the front office.

Price reporters don't just record what happened in the market. They assess what they believe a fair transaction would look like, based on the available evidence. That distinction matters when the market is thin and a small number of participants are determining the reference price for millions of barrels.

Every physical commodity contract references a price assessment. Understanding which benchmark applies, how it is calculated, and what drives divergence between assessments helps you evaluate contract terms, identify settlement disputes, and assess the quality of a mark-to-market price in an ETRM system.
d.pullQuote: Price reporters don't just record what happened in the market. They assess what they believe a fair transaction would look like, based on the available evidence. That distinction matters when the market is thin and a small number of participants are determining the reference price for millions of barrels.
d.handoff: Section D.5 covers supply disruption analysis — how the desk interprets an unplanned outage or supply shock and decides how to respond commercially.

d.title: Supply Disruption Analysis
d.desc: How the desk responds to unplanned outages and supply events in real time.
d.hook: An LNG train trips offline. A pipeline blows. A hurricane shuts the US Gulf. In the next 60 minutes, three things happen simultaneously: the physical market responds, the paper market reprices, and every desk capable of moving a cargo starts running the economics.
paragraphs: When a supply disruption occurs, the desk's first question is not 'how much will the price move?' but 'how much supply is actually at risk, for how long, and can it be replaced?' This **disruption magnitude assessment** requires understanding the scale of the affected facility, the timeline for restart (planned maintenance vs. unplanned trip), the inventory buffer at the impacted destination, and the availability of alternative supply from other sources.

The second question is 'what cargo diversion opportunities does this create?' A 3-week LNG plant outage in Australia reduces supply to Asian buyers. If they cannot wait for the plant to restart, they must source spot cargoes from the Atlantic Basin — pushing JKM up. If the JKM/TTF spread widens beyond the freight cost of rerouting Atlantic cargoes, those cargoes will flow east. The desk that has already mapped the available Atlantic tonnage and the logistics of rerouting it can move within hours of the disruption announcement.

The third question is 'how will the disruption resolve, and what happens to the price then?' Temporary supply disruptions that are quickly resolved can create sharp price spikes followed by equally sharp reversals. Desks that buy into a disruption spike without considering the timeline to restoration risk being caught on the wrong side of the reversal. The best disruption plays balance the near-term upside from the supply shortfall against the medium-term risk of restoration — and size positions accordingly.

The disruption is the trigger. The question that determines whether you make money is not how big the disruption is — it's whether you can source the replacement supply before anyone else does and get it to the right place before the window closes.

Supply disruption analysis is a core skill for commodity analysts and market intelligence professionals — but it also matters for schedulers (who manage cargo programmes when supply changes), risk managers (who need to re-assess positions when a disruption changes the market), and commercial managers (who may need to invoke force majeure clauses). Understanding the full chain of commercial implications from a single supply disruption is a strong demonstration of commercial awareness in any interview.
d.pullQuote: The disruption is the trigger. The question that determines whether you make money is not how big the disruption is — it's whether you can source the replacement supply before anyone else does and get it to the right place before the window closes.
d.handoff: Section D.6 covers positioning data — what speculative flows and COT reports tell a physical trader about market sentiment beyond the fundamental data.

d.title: Positioning Data & Speculative Flows
d.desc: What COT reports and open interest tell a physical trader about market sentiment.
d.hook: Fundamentals tell you what should happen to prices. Positioning data tells you what the money is already doing about it. Sometimes the gap between those two tells you more than either one alone.
paragraphs: The US CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission) publishes the **Commitments of Traders (COT) report** every Friday, covering positions held by different categories of market participants in NYMEX and CBOT futures markets. The report breaks positions into commercial hedgers (physical market participants), non-commercial speculators (managed money, hedge funds), and swap dealers. The net long or short position of non-commercial participants — the speculative community — is the number most closely watched by physical commodity traders.

When managed money builds an extremely large net long position in crude futures, the physical market is not always as bullish as the position implies — speculative money can be moved by momentum, sentiment, and macro factors that are disconnected from physical supply and demand. Conversely, when speculative shorts are at record levels, even a small bullish fundamental surprise can trigger a sharp short-covering rally as speculators exit positions simultaneously. Physical traders use COT data to calibrate how much of the current price reflects genuine physical tightness versus speculative positioning.

**Open interest** — the total number of outstanding futures contracts — is a complementary signal. Rising open interest alongside rising prices suggests new money is entering the market on the long side — a genuine bullish signal. Rising open interest alongside falling prices suggests new short positions are being built — a bearish signal. Falling open interest alongside price moves suggests existing positions are being closed — a reversal may be imminent.

When managed money is record long and the fundamental picture doesn't support it, the risk is not that you're wrong on the fundamental — it's that you're right on the fundamental but wrong on the timing because the speculative unwind happens before the physical tightness shows up in the price.

COT data is published weekly and free to access at cftc.gov. Building a habit of reading the weekly positioning report alongside the EIA report gives you a two-dimensional view of the crude market — one fundamental, one behavioural — that is more complete than either alone.
d.pullQuote: When managed money is record long and the fundamental picture doesn't support it, the risk is not that you're wrong on the fundamental — it's that you're right on the fundamental but wrong on the timing because the speculative unwind happens before the physical tightness shows up in the price.
d.handoff: Section D.7 covers seasonal demand patterns — the predictable, recurring demand shifts that create recurring trading opportunities if you know where to look.

d.title: Seasonal Patterns & Demand Calendars
d.desc: How time of year shapes commodity demand and where the recurring opportunities sit.
d.hook: Commodity markets repeat themselves every year. Not perfectly — but predictably enough that a trader who understands seasonal patterns consistently positions for moves the rest of the market treats as surprises.
paragraphs: Every commodity has a **demand calendar** — a seasonal pattern driven by weather, consumption cycles, and industrial activity. Crude oil and gasoline peak in summer (US driving season), creating a seasonal draw in gasoline stocks and widening gasoline crack spreads from March to August. Distillates and heating oil peak in winter, with Northern Hemisphere temperatures driving demand from October to February. Naphtha demand in Asia peaks in spring when petrochemical plants ramp up ethylene production.

LNG seasonal patterns are driven by the heating and cooling needs of end consumers. Northeast Asian LNG demand peaks in winter (December–February) for heating and in summer (July–August) for air conditioning. European LNG demand surges when pipeline gas supply is constrained — particularly in Q4 as storage is refilled. Australian LNG exports increase when maintenance windows close and production ramps back up after the southern hemisphere winter.

Seasonal patterns create predictable trading opportunities — but the opportunity is in the **deviation from the seasonal expectation**, not the seasonal move itself. A warm winter in Europe that reduces heating demand below seasonal norms will push TTF lower than the forward curve implied — and a trader positioned for this deviation earns from the correction. The baseline seasonal expectation is already priced into the market; the alpha comes from correctly forecasting where the actual demand will deviate from that baseline.

Seasonality is already in the price. The edge is not in knowing that driving season boosts gasoline — everyone knows that. The edge is in knowing whether this year's driving season will be stronger or weaker than the market's seasonal assumption.

Building a seasonal commodity calendar — tracking actual demand vs. seasonal expectations across crude, LNG, and refined products week by week — is one of the most practical things you can do to develop market intelligence skills before you join the industry. The data is available free from EIA, the IEA, and the Baltic Exchange.
d.pullQuote: Seasonality is already in the price. The edge is not in knowing that driving season boosts gasoline — everyone knows that. The edge is in knowing whether this year's driving season will be stronger or weaker than the market's seasonal assumption.
d.handoff: Section D.8 brings all the intelligence tools together in a practical framework — how to build a personal market intelligence workflow that surfaces signal from noise.

d.title: Building a Market Intelligence Workflow
d.desc: The tools, data sources, and daily habits the desk actually uses to stay ahead of the market.
d.hook: Market intelligence is not about having access to more data than anyone else. It is about having the right data, processed in the right order, at the right time of day — so you see the signal that matters before the rest of the market does.
paragraphs: A structured market intelligence workflow starts with a **morning read** — the data sources and signals a trader checks before markets open. This typically includes: overnight price moves in flat price and key differentials, any AIS signals from Kpler or Vortexa showing unexpected vessel movements, any significant news events overnight (supply disruptions, geopolitical developments, demand updates), and a review of the desk's own position against current market levels. The morning read should take no more than 30 minutes — its purpose is situation awareness, not analysis.

During the trading day, the desk tracks a specific set of **live signals** relevant to their commodity and position. For a crude desk, this includes Brent prompt month price, the Brent/WTI spread, the Dubai/Brent differential, VLCC freight rates on key routes, and any breaking supply news. For an LNG desk, this includes JKM, TTF, the JKM/TTF spread, LNG carrier hire rates, and Australian send-out data. The specific signals vary by commodity and market — but the principle is the same: a small set of indicators, monitored continuously, from which unusual moves trigger deeper investigation.

The **weekly cadence** anchors around the recurring data releases: EIA petroleum status report (Wednesday), EIA natural gas storage (Thursday), Baltic Exchange Friday indices, and CFTC COT report (Friday close, published the following Friday). Building a weekly analytical routine around these releases — preparing expectations in advance and comparing them to actuals — is the discipline that separates informed market participants from reactive ones.

The best intelligence edge is not real-time data — it is having thought about the question before the data arrives. Preparing your expectation in advance means you can assess the actual number in 10 seconds instead of 10 minutes. In volatile markets, those 9 minutes and 50 seconds are where the money is.

The market intelligence workflow described in this section is something you can begin building immediately — before you enter the industry. Set up free data alerts for Brent and WTI on your phone. Bookmark eia.gov and cftc.gov and check them weekly. Create a simple spreadsheet tracking EIA actuals vs. consensus each Wednesday. After 12 weeks, you will have built a habit and a dataset that demonstrates genuine market engagement to any interviewer.
d.pullQuote: The best intelligence edge is not real-time data — it is having thought about the question before the data arrives. Preparing your expectation in advance means you can assess the actual number in 10 seconds instead of 10 minutes. In volatile markets, those 9 minutes and 50 seconds are where the money is.

e.title: How a Trader Thinks
e.desc: The mental model behind every commercial decision — thesis, exit, downside.
e.hook: A trade idea and a trade are two very different things. Most people in and around commodity markets have plenty of trade ideas. The discipline is in knowing which ones to act on — and how.
paragraphs: Before entering any position, an experienced commodity trader asks three questions. First: **What is my thesis?** Not 'I think crude will go up' — that is not a thesis. A thesis is a specific causal argument: EIA data will show three consecutive bullish draws next month because refinery utilisation is rising faster than import volumes are replacing the Libyan production shortfall. A good thesis names the cause, the mechanism, and the expected market response.

Second: **What is my exit?** Every position should have a defined exit point before it is entered — both the target (the price level at which the thesis is proven and profits are taken) and the stop (the price level at which the thesis is disproven and losses are cut). A position without an exit plan will inevitably be held too long on the losing side and exited too early on the winning side, because human psychology pushes in both directions simultaneously.

Third: **What is my downside?** The trader calculates the maximum loss they would accept if the thesis is wrong — and sizes the position so that this loss is within their risk limits and their own tolerance for being wrong. A high-conviction trade in a liquid market with a clear stop might justify a full position. A speculative view in a thin market without a clear catalyst might justify 20% of that position.

The three questions are not bureaucratic. They are the difference between trading and gambling. Gambling is taking a position because you feel like it might work. Trading is taking a position because you have a thesis, an exit, and a clearly defined maximum loss.

These three questions apply to any commercial decision — not just futures trades. Before presenting a market view, a deal structure, or an operational recommendation, ask yourself: what is my thesis, what would disprove it, and what is the maximum cost if I am wrong? Structuring your thinking this way makes you significantly more persuasive and more rigorous simultaneously.
e.pullQuote: The three questions are not bureaucratic. They are the difference between trading and gambling. Gambling is taking a position because you feel like it might work. Trading is taking a position because you have a thesis, an exit, and a clearly defined maximum loss.
e.handoff: Section E.2 applies this framework to the most visible commercial opportunity in physical commodity markets — the arbitrage window.

e.title: The Arbitrage Window
e.desc: How regional price gaps open, close, and get exploited in physical commodity markets.
e.hook: The arbitrage window is the physical commodity market's most time-sensitive opportunity. When a price gap between two markets exceeds the cost of bridging them, money flows toward the higher-priced market until the gap closes. The desk that moves first captures the margin. The desk that moves second finds the window already closed.
paragraphs: An **arbitrage window** opens when the price differential between two regional markets for the same commodity exceeds the total cost of moving a cargo from the lower-priced market to the higher-priced one. The calculation is straightforward in principle: Gross spread − freight − port costs − boil-off − credit margin = net arb margin. A positive net arb margin means the window is open; a negative margin means it is not viable.

The forces that open a window are the same forces that close it — because exploiting the arb is what closes it. When Atlantic Basin LNG desks divert cargoes toward Asia to capture a wide JKM/TTF spread, those additional cargoes increase supply in Asia (pushing JKM down) and reduce supply in Europe (pushing TTF up). Simultaneously, the increased demand for LNG carriers on the long Asia route pushes freight rates higher — further compressing the net arb margin. The window closes not because the fundamental imbalance resolves, but because the act of exploiting it resolves the imbalance.

Speed of execution is the primary determinant of whether a desk captures an arb or watches it close. The four capabilities that determine execution speed are: freight access (vessel availability and pre-fixed rates), counterparty network (a buyer at the destination who can commit quickly), contractual flexibility (DES contracts with destination flexibility or spot cargoes with no destination restriction), and internal approval speed (the ability to get commercial approval without bureaucratic delay).

The arb window is not a gift. It is a race. By the time most of the market knows it's open, the fastest desks are already fixing vessels. Speed and preparation — not analysis after the fact — determine who captures the margin.

Understanding the arbitrage mechanism is the single most direct answer to the interview question 'how do commodity trading desks make money?' Being able to explain — with a specific example and worked numbers — how a regional price gap opens, how it is calculated, and why it closes naturally demonstrates commercial intelligence in a way that generic answers about supply and demand do not.
e.pullQuote: The arb window is not a gift. It is a race. By the time most of the market knows it's open, the fastest desks are already fixing vessels. Speed and preparation — not analysis after the fact — determine who captures the margin.
e.handoff: Section E.3 provides the decision framework for the most consequential and time-pressured version of the arb decision — the mid-voyage cargo diversion.

e.title: The Cargo Diversion Decision Tree
e.desc: The full commercial logic for rerouting a vessel mid-voyage — with a downloadable decision framework.
e.hook: A cargo diversion is the most compressed commercial decision in physical commodity trading. In the time it takes to make the call — hours, sometimes less — the spread may have already narrowed, the freight rates may have moved, and the best counterparty may have already committed to another desk.
paragraphs: The cargo diversion decision begins with a spread calculation — but the spread alone is not sufficient to make the call. The desk must work through a sequence of questions simultaneously: Is the spread wide enough after all costs? Is a suitable vessel available at the assumed freight rate? Does the contractual structure of the cargo allow diversion — is it DES with destination flexibility, or FOB where the original buyer controls the vessel? If the original buyer must release the cargo, what is their compensation demand?

The second layer of the decision covers operational feasibility. Can the vessel reach the new destination within the available loading or delivery window? Is the receiving terminal at the new destination available and capable of accepting the cargo — correct draft, regasification capacity, product specification compatibility? Is the counterparty at the new destination creditworthy and able to commit immediately? Each question must be answered before committing to the diversion — because reversing a diversion decision mid-execution is extremely costly.

The third layer covers risk management. What is the P&L sensitivity to the spread narrowing by 20% after the decision is made? What happens to the position if freight rates move further against the desk after the vessel is re-fixed? Is the diversion approved within the desk's position limits and VaR framework? A diversion that looks compelling on a base-case calculation may be unacceptable once stress scenarios are applied — and the risk manager's involvement in this assessment is not optional.

The diversion decision is not one question — it's twelve questions, asked in parallel, with a clock running. The desks that answer them fastest and most completely are the ones that capture the margin. Preparation — mapping the answers to each question before the market moves — is the only way to be fast enough.

The cargo diversion decision tree is one of the most comprehensive commercial decision frameworks in commodity trading — and demonstrating that you understand every question in it is one of the strongest signals of commercial intelligence you can send in any interview for a trading, origination, or analytics role.
e.pullQuote: The diversion decision is not one question — it's twelve questions, asked in parallel, with a clock running. The desks that answer them fastest and most completely are the ones that capture the margin. Preparation — mapping the answers to each question before the market moves — is the only way to be fast enough.
e.handoff: Section E.4 covers timing — specifically the hedge timing decision that determines whether the desk removes price risk before or after price moves against it.

e.title: Timing a Hedge
e.desc: How desks manage price risk between when a cargo is booked and when it is delivered.
e.hook: The hedge decision is not binary — it is continuous. The question is not whether to hedge but when, how much, and at what price. Getting all three right is the edge that separates the best risk managers from the rest.
paragraphs: When a physical trader buys a cargo, they immediately carry price risk — the risk that the commodity price falls before they sell it. They can hedge that risk by selling futures or swaps. But the decision of **when to hedge** is commercially significant. A trader who hedges immediately locks in the current price and removes all subsequent risk — but also removes all subsequent upside. A trader who delays hedging retains price exposure, hoping to sell the hedge at a better level — but risks the price moving further against them.

The **hedge ratio** — what percentage of the physical position is hedged with paper — is equally important. A 100% hedge is fully protected but captures no upside. A 50% hedge retains significant exposure. Mandatory hedge ratios enforced by risk policy remove trader discretion; desks with more flexible risk mandates allow traders to choose their hedge ratio based on their market view and risk appetite. Some desks hedge in tranches — placing 40% of the hedge immediately, then adding to it as the market evolves.

**Basis risk** affects the effectiveness of every hedge. If a West African crude cargo is hedged with ICE Brent futures, the hedge is effective only to the extent that the WA differential to Dated Brent remains stable. If the differential widens — WA crude weakens relative to Brent — the physical cargo loses value more than the futures hedge gains. The trader is exposed to the differential move despite being 'hedged' on flat price. Managing basis risk requires either hedging the differential separately or accepting that a proportion of the position will always be unhedged.

Being perfectly hedged means giving up all your upside to remove your downside. Most desks don't want that — they want to be selectively hedged, protecting against the bad scenario while retaining some ability to benefit if the view is right.

Hedge timing and hedge ratio decisions are made by traders — but they are evaluated by risk managers, implemented by the back office, and their effectiveness is assessed by finance. Understanding the full cycle of a hedging decision — from commercial logic through to ETRM booking and P&L attribution — makes you more effective in any function around the desk.
e.pullQuote: Being perfectly hedged means giving up all your upside to remove your downside. Most desks don't want that — they want to be selectively hedged, protecting against the bad scenario while retaining some ability to benefit if the view is right.
e.handoff: Section E.5 shows what the P&L of a hedged physical position actually looks like — mapping every dollar of profit or loss to one of the six commercial levers.

e.title: The P&L Attribution Map
e.desc: Where trading profit actually comes from — all six levers mapped to a real cargo.
e.hook: Most trading P&L reports say 'crude trading made $X million this month.' What they don't say is how much of that came from flat price calls, how much came from basis, how much came from freight, and how much came from optionality. The attribution is where the real commercial intelligence lives.
paragraphs: P&L attribution is the process of decomposing a trading desk's profit or loss into its component sources. For a physical commodity desk running multiple concurrent positions, the total P&L in any period is the sum of contributions from: **flat price moves** (the change in value due to the overall price level moving), **time spread** (value earned or lost from holding positions across different delivery dates), **location differential** (value from moving commodity between markets), **quality differential** (value from the grade premium or discount), **freight** (P&L from freight positions relative to market), and **optionality** (value from flexibility provisions in contracts or vessel charters).

On any given trade, some levers contribute positively and others negatively. A cargo that made money overall might have lost $500,000 on flat price (the market moved against the trader), gained $800,000 on location differential (the destination market was stronger than expected), and gained $300,000 on freight (rates were fixed below market). The net $600,000 profit came not from being right on the flat price — where the desk was wrong — but from being right on the basis and the freight.

Understanding P&L attribution matters for multiple reasons. Risk managers use it to assess which positions are generating alpha and which are just lucky flat price bets. Traders use it to evaluate their own edge — are they consistently making money on basis, or consistently losing on freight? Analysts use it to build better models — if freight is consistently misforecast, the model needs improvement. Attribution transforms a P&L number into a learning tool.
The P&L number tells you whether you made money. The attribution tells you why — and why matters enormously, because a desk that makes money for the wrong reasons will eventually make money for none.

P&L attribution is a back-office and risk function in most firms, but the commercial logic behind it is essential for analysts, traders, and anyone evaluating the performance of a trading strategy. Being able to look at a P&L report and ask 'which lever generated this?' demonstrates a level of commercial sophistication that most candidates cannot match.
e.pullQuote: The P&L number tells you whether you made money. The attribution tells you why — and why matters enormously, because a desk that makes money for the wrong reasons will eventually make money for none.
e.handoff: Section E.6 covers the risk management framework that surrounds all of these positions — VaR, limits, and how risk managers and traders interact when positions approach the boundary.

e.title: VaR, Limits & Risk Management
e.desc: How the desk measures and controls its combined market exposure in real time.
e.hook: A trading desk without risk limits is not a trading desk — it is a fund. The limits are not constraints on ambition. They are the infrastructure that allows ambition to persist through the inevitable periods when the market is wrong about what you're right about.
paragraphs: **Value at Risk (VaR)** is the industry-standard metric for measuring commodity trading desk market risk. It estimates the maximum loss a portfolio of positions could suffer over a defined time horizon (typically 1 day or 10 days) at a defined confidence level (typically 95% or 99%). A VaR of $8 million at 95% confidence over one day means the desk should not expect to lose more than $8 million on 95% of trading days — or roughly 19 out of every 20 trading days.

VaR is calculated daily using historical price data and the current position. As positions change and market volatility changes, VaR changes — a large position in a highly volatile market may generate the same VaR as a larger position in a less volatile one. Risk managers set **VaR limits** for the desk, individual traders, and specific commodities or strategies. When a position approaches a limit, the risk manager flags it and may require the trader to reduce exposure — regardless of whether the trader believes the position is correct.

Beyond VaR, desks manage **position limits** (maximum notional exposure in a commodity), **stop-loss limits** (the maximum daily or monthly loss before the desk must reduce positions), and **stress test results** (how the portfolio performs under severe but plausible scenarios — e.g., a $30/bbl crude price move over 5 days). Each of these limits serves a different purpose: VaR manages routine risk, stop-losses prevent loss escalation, and stress tests protect against tail events that VaR underestimates.

Risk management is not about preventing the desk from losing money. It is about ensuring that no single loss — however bad — can threaten the firm's ability to continue operating. The limit protects the institution, not the trader.

Risk management is a discipline in its own right — and a growing function in every commodity trading firm as regulatory requirements increase. Even if you are targeting a front-office role, understanding VaR, limits, and the risk manager's role demonstrates the commercial maturity that senior hiring managers value. And if you are targeting a risk or middle-office role, this section is your starting point for a much deeper specialisation.
e.pullQuote: Risk management is not about preventing the desk from losing money. It is about ensuring that no single loss — however bad — can threaten the firm's ability to continue operating. The limit protects the institution, not the trader.
e.handoff: Section E.7 addresses the hardest skill in commodity trading — knowing when a position is wrong and cutting it cleanly, without the emotional distortions that turn small losses into large ones.

e.title: When the Trade Goes Wrong
e.desc: Stop-loss discipline, loss management, and how desks cut positions without emotional bias.
e.hook: Losing money is not the failure. Failing to cut a losing position when the thesis is disproven is the failure. The distinction between those two things is the most important discipline in commodity trading — and the one that most people, at every level of experience, consistently struggle with.
paragraphs: When a position moves against the desk, there are two possibilities: the thesis is wrong, or the thesis is early. A position that is **wrong** should be cut — the evidence has changed, the market is telling you something you didn't know, and holding on increases the loss without improving the odds of recovery. A position that is **early** may be worth holding — the thesis is still intact, the fundamental picture supports the view, and the market will eventually confirm it. The challenge is that under loss pressure, these two states feel identical — and human psychology consistently misclassifies wrong positions as early ones.

**Stop-loss discipline** is the practice of committing to a maximum loss on a position before entering it and cutting the position automatically when that loss is reached — without re-evaluating the thesis under the influence of the current loss. The stop-loss is not a prediction about what the market will do at that level; it is a commitment about how much of the thesis you are willing to fund before accepting that it is disproven. A trader who consistently moves their stop-loss further away from entry is not showing flexibility — they are demonstrating the inability to accept being wrong.

The **communication of losses** up the management chain is a distinct skill from loss management itself. A position that has moved significantly against the desk must be reported promptly, with a clear account of the current thesis status (wrong or early), the remaining exposure, and the plan for managing it. Traders who delay reporting losses — hoping the position will recover before they have to explain it — universally make the situation worse. Risk managers who discover losses that were not reported promptly lose trust in the trader permanently.

The stop-loss is not there to tell you when the market is wrong. It is there to tell you when you are. The willingness to act on that information, without flinching, is the single most important risk management discipline on any desk.

The psychology of loss and the discipline of cutting positions are relevant to every function that makes recommendations — not just traders. An analyst who does not revisit a view when the evidence changes, an originator who does not walk away from a deal when the economics deteriorate, a scheduler who does not flag an operational problem early enough — all exhibit the same failure mode as a trader who won't cut a losing position. The discipline is universal.

e.title: A Week on the Desk — Putting It All Together
e.desc: A narrative case study of a complete trading week — connecting every skill from the Playbook to a live commercial scenario.
e.hook: Everything in the Playbook has been building to this. One week, one desk, one set of markets — and every commercial decision made in real time, with the information available at the time, not the benefit of hindsight.
paragraphs: The scenario is a crude oil trading desk at a mid-sized commodity trading firm. It is Monday morning. The desk carries a net long position of 3 million barrels of North Sea Brent crude against ICE futures hedges. The hedge ratio is 80% — 20% of the position is open to flat price. The prior week's EIA report showed a 2.1 million barrel crude draw against a consensus estimate of 0.9 million — a bullish surprise. Brent is trading at $81.50, up $1.20 from Friday's close. The forward curve is in modest backwardation — M1 at $81.50, M3 at $80.20. The desk also has a VLCC fixed at WS95 on the Middle East Gulf–Rotterdam route, loading next Thursday.

**Monday:** The desk reviews overnight developments — news of an unplanned shutdown at a North Sea production platform has reduced expected loadings by approximately 500,000 barrels over the next two weeks. The fundamental case for the long position strengthens. The trader increases the open position from 20% to 35% by buying back some of the ICE hedge. Risk management flags the increased VaR. The trader provides the thesis: supply disruption tightens the near-term physical balance; the backwardation should steepen. The risk manager approves within limits. **Wednesday:** EIA report. The desk's expectation was a 1.5 million barrel draw based on the production platform news and the prior week's trend. Actual: a 3.8 million barrel draw. Brent rallies $2.40 in 15 minutes. The trader increases the hedge from 65% to 85% — locking in the majority of the week's gain. The forward curve moves into stronger backwardation.

**Thursday:** The VLCC loads at Ras Tanura. During loading, the independent surveyor finds a quality issue — sulphur content marginally above specification. The scheduling team negotiates a small price adjustment with the Rotterdam receiver. The cargo is accepted; demurrage of 14 hours is accrued during the inspection delay. **Friday:** The position is reviewed. The open position is reduced to 15% ahead of the weekend. Net P&L for the week: $4.2 million. Attribution: $2.8M from flat price (backwardation trade worked); $0.9M from time spread (front of curve strengthened relative to back); -$0.3M from basis (North Sea physical/ICE differential widened); $0.8M from freight (WS95 fixture below current WS110 market); -$0.1M from demurrage (operationally avoidable).

A good week on the desk is not one where everything goes perfectly. It is one where the thesis was sound, the risk was controlled, the losses were small and understood, and the gains reflected genuine commercial skill — not luck.

The skills that determined the outcomes in each day of this week — view formation, hedge timing, supply disruption analysis, scheduling coordination, freight positioning, and P&L attribution — are the skills covered in all five chapters of this Playbook. If you can follow the commercial logic of each decision in this case study and articulate why each choice was made, you have achieved the core learning objective of the Full Playbook.
